So BDCs just take a step back.
It stands for Business Development Companies.
They've been around for quite a while.
They've actually been around since 1980 as an amendment to the Investment Company Act
And what their purpose was and still is, is to lend to medium and small businesses, primarily
in the US.
So think of them like banks without actually the deposits.
So how they get their capital to lend out is primarily three ways.
They issue bonds to the public market, they issue equity, and they also sometimes have
a direct line of credit as well.
And then they lend these loans out to small and medium-sized companies, primarily floating
rate loans, which is now their asset side.
And they make money off the spread of what they borrow on and what they can lend on.
They were always kind of a small part of the market historically.
But after the great financial crisis of 1809 and banking regulation really stepped up quite
a bit.
BDCs filled a lot of the void that was left after the crisis in 2009.
So BDC assets have grown pretty substantially over the last 15 or so years.
And many folks know BDCs on the equity side.
BizD, for example, is a very large ETF that tracks BDC equity.
But there was nothing out there that tracked the BDC bonds themselves.
So these are bonds that are directly issued by the BDCs themselves that are used to finance
the loans that they make in these small and medium-sized companies.
What kind of attracted us to the space is, like I mentioned at Hilton, we've been running
our tactical income strategy, which is about two and a half billion of assets for over
25 years now, and have owned several of these bonds in the past.
They're pretty short duration bonds, typically three to five years duration, and they have

They're typically about 200 to 300 basis points over like-duration treasuries, 100 to 200

So we've owned them for quite a while, and running the strategies, we said, hey, you

So we said, hey, you know what?
Let's wrap this up in an ETF.
Let's make a really detail oriented index.
There was no index out there, and then let's track it and launch this ETF.
So now HBDC is the first and only pure play bond BDC and ETF out there.
And when we constructed the index, we partnered with a German company called Selective.
They're pretty large.
They do a lot of indexes out there.
And given that most of these BDC bonds are overwhelmingly the very large guys, as you
can imagine, like the Aries, the Blue Owls of the world out there, we didn't want it
to be overly concentrated in those BDCs themselves.
So we actually capped the top two largest issuers at 10%, and then the second largest
issuers at eight, and then the following two at seven, and then everybody else is capped
at five.
So the index itself and the ETF by and large actually overweights the smaller BDCs by design

It's almost 95% investment grade bonds.

So we've been seeing in the news a lot about private credit.

How does owning BDC bonds, given investors, never heard of a BDC bond, like access in
a way to that market?
Yeah.
So I like to say it's tangentant to the private credit market.
This ETF does not own the direct loans that these BDCs are making to these small and medium
sized companies.
It's the bonds that they're issuing to get the capital so they can then lend out to these
small and medium sized companies.
But that actually has some structural protections in place and why we like these bonds.
So BDCs, by law, actually can only leverage up their balance sheets a max two to one.
So what that means is for every $2 of debt, they have to have a dollar of equity cushion
below it.
That's in comparison to banks that are levered at eight to one or even larger than that.
So when you buy a bank bond, you're essentially buying a balance sheet that's levered eight
to one, and no one really bats an eye on some of these large cap banks.
So there's substantially more equity cushion on these BDCs, and most BDCs, including the
large ones, like I mentioned, Aries and so forth, run their balance sheets significantly
more conservatively than their max statutory leverage ratios.
Most of them are one to one or even less than one to one.
So there's a lot of cushion in place.
So just to kind of conceptualize that, if you run your balance sheet at a max two to
one ratio, you would need a 50% drawdown on the nav before the bonds would start to be
impaired, which is a pretty substantial credit event and has actually never happened throughout
the history of BDCs existing.
And going back all the way to 1980, there has never been a BDC bond impairment.
So there's been many credit cycles since 1980, and these bonds have held up quite well.

So if you look at a cap structure of a BDC or really any company, because a BDC is just
a company at the end of the day, you have equity, which is right at the bottom of the
Tron structure.
So those guys that if when you're owning BISD and ARCC equity, yes, they have very large
dividends, but you're at the very bottom of the capital structure, meaning if there's
ever sort of an impairment to NAV and so forth, you're the first ones that are taking the losses.
Then on top of the equity, you sometimes have preferred equity or convertible preferreds
as well.
Those typically, if you have a significant event, obviously like a Chapter 11 type of
process, those would get wiped out as well.
And then on top of that, that's where BDC bonds sit is the senior unsecured bonds.
And then within bonds themselves, sometimes you have senior unsecured and you have junior
and so forth.
All these bonds in our portfolio are senior unsecured.
So they're on the very, very top of the bond structure, meaning that they sit pretty high
up there.
There are, however, sometimes not all BDCs, but some companies do secured bonds, meaning
that they're tied directly to some sort of asset on their balance sheet.
So those would sit above that.
And then if there's any sort of secured direct lending or so forth line of credit, that would
sit at the very, very top.
So when you look at a cap structure, I would say BDC bonds in HBDC sit towards the middle
or higher portion of the capital structure.
So there's a lot of cushion below these bonds.
So like we mentioned, you would need a significant credit event to even get, be worried about
these bonds.
And that's kind of the opportunity here because the spreads and the yields maturities on these

So well, within any ETF and with our ETF as well, you have creation and redemption units.
So what that is is we have a lead market maker that would buy these securities or they could

So what that does is even if there is, let's say, a million dollars in the ETF, which we

The lead market maker would then buy all the bonds in the portfolio and then structure
